claims.text: A coherent or semi-coherent, magnetically hard or exchange-coupled secondary phase within an fcc matrix will enable coercivity above 100 Oe.
Ti can drive precipitation of a Ti-rich L12 or B2 intermetallic or a Ti-stabilized BCC phase within the fcc matrix.
The Ti-rich secondary phase will act as a magnetic-domain-wall pinning center.
Strain fields and chemical-potential gradients at fcc/precipitate boundaries may enhance the local orbital moment or create strong exchange coupling.
The proposed Fe-Co-Ni-Ti starting alloy can be single-phase fcc at room temperature while remaining prone to thermally induced phase separation.
Solution annealing at 1100°C for 1 hour will homogenize the proposed alloy.
Aging at 600–700°C for 10–20 hours will induce Ti-rich precipitation while avoiding excessive coarsening.
In AlCoFeNi-based alloys, lower-temperature annealing produces fine phase decomposition and higher coercivity than the single ordered phase obtained at 1000°C.
The treatment will produce Ti-rich BCC or L12 precipitates with sizes of 5–50 nm in the fcc matrix.
Local strain fields and chemical discontinuities around the secondary phase increase the energy barrier for domain-wall motion and therefore increase coercivity.
A hierarchical distribution of precipitate length scales will pin domain walls at multiple scales and prevent easy depinning.
Ti is critical for stabilizing the secondary phase and may enhance the magnetic anisotropy of the precipitate.
The aged Ti-containing fcc alloy will exhibit coercivity above 100 Oe.
Aging will slightly reduce saturation magnetization because the Ti-rich precipitates are nonmagnetic or weakly magnetic.
The magnetic ordering temperature will remain above 400 K because of the high Fe and Co content of the matrix.
The unaged single-phase fcc FeCoNiTi baseline will have coercivity below 10 Oe because of orbital-moment suppression and the absence of domain-wall pinning sites.
Ti concentrations of 5–20 at.% favor secondary-phase precipitation without completely consuming the fcc matrix.
Excessive Ti may transform the matrix into a nonmagnetic or brittle BCC or sigma phase and destroy the fcc magnetic ground state.
Precipitates larger than 100 nm or smaller than 2 nm will not effectively pin domain walls.
A coercivity of approximately 40 Oe was observed in a phase-separated AlCo0.5Cr0.5FeNi alloy.
